sessions.title: A direction the map does not turn away
sessions.focus: Define eigenvectors/eigenvalues from invariant one-dimensional directions, distinguish direction preservation from fixed vectors or preserved length, and derive repeated action along one eigenvector.
sessions.purpose: M14 taught what a linear map does to arbitrary vectors. M16 begins by asking whether any nonzero directions are special enough that the map only rescales them; the concept must exist before the characteristic-polynomial recipe.
sessions.centralCapability: Given a finite real linear map and fresh candidate vectors, verify or refute eigenvector status from Av=λv, interpret the invariant line, and use λ to predict repeated action along that direction.
sessions.principalObstacle: A learner may confuse Av=v with Av=λv, preserved norm with preserved direction, or allow v=0 because A0=λ0 for every λ.
entryPrerequisites: M13 nonzero vectors, scalar multiples and span(v)
M14 matrix-vector action and finite linear maps
M02/M09 scalar powers for repeated action
requiredOwnership: Verify eigenpair status Av=λv for supplied nonzero real candidates by exact proportionality, recovering λ when it exists.
Use linearity to justify that a nonzero scalar rescaling of a verified eigenvector represents the same eigendirection and retains the same eigenvalue.
Distinguish preserved direction from fixed-vector or preserved-length claims and use a verified eigenpair to justify a specified repeated action A^k v=λ^k v.
sessions.applicationScope: Exact finite real 2D/3D linear maps; candidate directions are checked directly without characteristic polynomials.
sessions.transferScope: Audit an orthogonal rotation that preserves length but has no nonzero real eigenvector, forcing the learner to reject preserved-length reasoning.
inScope: repeated action on a verified eigenvector
sessions.exitCondition: On a fresh linear map, verify/refute candidate eigenvectors, identify λ when it exists, explain the invariant line and use the verified eigenpair to predict repeated action without matrix-power brute force.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. M14 taught us to apply a linear map to any vector. Now ask a more structural question: is there a nonzero direction that the map does not turn away from itself? If A sends a nonzero vector v to a scalar multiple of itself, Av=λv, then v is an eigenvector and λ is its eigenvalue. The line span(v) is invariant because every point cv on that line is sent to A(cv)=cAv=cλv, which is still on the same line.

Definition discipline. The vector must be nonzero. If v=0 were admitted, A0=λ0 would hold for every λ and the word eigenvalue would stop identifying anything. The scalar λ is allowed to be zero: for P=diag(1,0), e2=(0,1) is nonzero and Pe2=0=0e2. A negative λ reverses orientation along the same line; |λ|>1 stretches and |λ|<1 shrinks. Only λ=1 makes every eigenvector on that line a fixed vector.

Worked example. Let A=[[2,1],[0,1]]. For e1=(1,0), Ae1=(2,0)=2e1, so e1 is an eigenvector with λ=2. For w=(1,-1), Aw=(1,-1)=w, so w is an eigenvector with λ=1. But e2=(0,1) maps to (1,1), which is not a scalar multiple of e2, so e2 is not an eigenvector. The decisive test is exact proportionality, not whether the image merely looks similar.

Connect. If Av=λv and c≠0, then A(cv)=cAv=cλv=λ(cv), so all nonzero vectors on the same invariant line share the same eigenvalue. This is about a direction/subspace, even though we represent it by particular nonzero vectors.

Repeated action. Once Av=λv, apply A again: A²v=A(λv)=λAv=λ²v. Induction gives A^k v=λ^k v for every integer k≥0. This conclusion is earned only after the eigenpair is verified.

Guided practice. Let C=[[3,0],[2,1]]. Test u=(1,1), v=(0,1), and r=(1,0). For every eigenvector, identify λ and the invariant line. Then predict C^4u without multiplying four matrices.

Fade. The fixed Main changes both the matrix and candidate directions; the Transfer changes the representation entirely to a rotation audit. No fixed answer is solved in the lesson.

Distinction check. Fixed vector means λ=1. Preserved length says ||Av||=||v||. Eigenvector says Av is exactly a real scalar multiple of the nonzero v. These are different properties.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. Cu=(3,3)=3u, so u has λ=3 and invariant line span(1,1). Cv=(0,1)=v, so v has λ=1 and invariant line span(0,1). Cr=(3,2) is not proportional to r, so r is not an eigenvector. Therefore C^4u=3^4u=81(1,1)=(81,81).

sessions.title: An eigenspace is a kernel
sessions.focus: Rewrite Av=λv as (A-λI)v=0, identify E_λ as a null space, and separate the eigenspace subspace from its nonzero eigenvectors.
sessions.purpose: S01 identified special directions one candidate at a time. S02 turns one verified eigenvalue into the full family of vectors sharing it, using M14 null-space structure before any characteristic-polynomial machinery appears.
sessions.centralCapability: For a supplied real λ, form A-λI, solve its homogeneous system, report a basis/span for E_λ, and distinguish the zero vector's membership in the eigenspace from the nonzero requirement for eigenvectors.
sessions.principalObstacle: The equation Av=λv is treated as a one-vector check rather than a homogeneous system; alternatively the zero vector is either wrongly excluded from E_λ or wrongly promoted to an eigenvector.
entryPrerequisites: S01 eigenpair definition and invariant line
M14 homogeneous systems and null spaces
requiredOwnership: For a supplied real λ, rewrite Av=λv as (A-λI)v=0 and compute E_λ=Null(A-λI) as a span/basis.
Distinguish the eigenspace E_λ, which is a subspace containing 0, from the set of eigenvectors for λ, which consists of the nonzero vectors in E_λ.
Audit whether a proposed set of eigenvectors is itself an eigenspace by checking subspace requirements and the zero-vector boundary.
sessions.applicationScope: Exact finite real square matrices with λ supplied; systematic discovery of λ remains S03.
sessions.transferScope: Audit a report that removes zero from a correct eigenline and then incorrectly calls the resulting set an eigenspace.
sessions.exitCondition: Given A and a supplied λ, compute the entire eigenspace and state exactly which members are eigenvectors.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. S01 let us test one candidate v. But once λ is known, we want every vector with that eigenvalue. Start from Av=λv and move all terms to one side: (A-λI)v=0. M14 already taught how to solve a homogeneous system, so the new object is built from an old one.

Define. For a fixed scalar λ, the eigenspace is E_λ={v:Av=λv}=Null(A-λI). Because every null space is a subspace, E_λ contains 0 and is closed under linear combinations. Eigenvectors for λ are the nonzero members of E_λ. So “eigenspace” and “set of eigenvectors” are not literally the same set.

Worked example. Let A=[[2,1],[0,2]] and suppose λ=2 is supplied. Then A-2I=[[0,1],[0,0]]. Solving (A-2I)(x,y)^T=0 gives y=0 and x free, so E_2=span{(1,0)}. Every nonzero (t,0) is an eigenvector with λ=2; (0,0) belongs to E_2 but is not an eigenvector. If instead λ=1 is supplied, A-I=[[1,1],[0,1]] has only the zero solution, so E_1={0}; therefore 1 is not an eigenvalue.

Connect. This uses no new elimination theorem. The only new move is recognizing the eigenvector equation as a null-space problem for the shifted matrix A-λI.

Guided practice. Let B=[[3,0,0],[0,3,1],[0,0,1]] and take λ=3. Form B-3I, solve the homogeneous system, give a basis for E_3, and state which vectors in that eigenspace are eigenvectors.

Fade. Main supplies a new 3x3 matrix and two λ values. Transfer stops being a calculation and instead asks whether a proposed punctured line is an eigenspace.

Distinction check. E_λ must include zero because it is a null space. The zero vector is nevertheless never called an eigenvector. If Null(A-λI)={0}, then there is no eigenvector for that λ.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. B-3I=[[0,0,0],[0,0,1],[0,0,-2]], so z=0 while x,y are free. Thus E_3=span{(1,0,0),(0,1,0)}. Every nonzero vector in this plane is an eigenvector with λ=3; the zero vector is in E_3 but is not an eigenvector.

sessions.title: Why the characteristic equation appears
sessions.focus: Derive det(A-λI)=0 from the need for a nonzero null-space solution, solve exact low-degree characteristic equations, and return to eigenspaces rather than stopping at roots.
sessions.purpose: S02 can recover E_λ once λ is supplied. S03 earns a systematic way to discover candidate λ values from M14 singularity/determinant structure without turning the determinant equation into the definition of eigenvalue.
sessions.centralCapability: Derive the characteristic equation from Av=λv and singularity, solve it for a small exact matrix, and compute the corresponding eigenspaces.
sessions.principalObstacle: The learner may memorize det(A-λI)=0 as a magic recipe, confuse det(A) with an eigenvalue, or stop after roots without verifying nonzero eigenspaces.
requiredOwnership: Derive det(A-λI)=0 from the requirement that (A-λI)v=0 have a nonzero solution.
Compute the characteristic polynomial/equation for an exact 2×2 or manageable triangular 3×3 matrix and solve for its real eigenvalues.
For each computed eigenvalue, return to Null(A-λI) to construct an eigenspace rather than treating a polynomial root alone as the full eigenpair result.
sessions.applicationScope: Exact small real square matrices whose characteristic polynomial is readily factorable or otherwise solvable with earlier algebra.
sessions.transferScope: Audit a report that mistakes det(A) itself for an eigenvalue and repair the complete eigenvalue/eigenspace analysis.
sessions.exitCondition: From a fresh small matrix, justify the determinant equation, solve the eigenvalues and recover every corresponding eigenspace.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. S02 answered: if λ is known, solve Null(A-λI). Now reverse the question. Which λ make that null space contain something besides 0?

Connect. M14 says a square matrix B has a nonzero solution to Bv=0 exactly when B is singular, and B is singular exactly when det(B)=0. Apply that theorem to the same object B=A-λI. Therefore Av=λv with v≠0 is possible exactly when det(A-λI)=0. This determinant equation is a consequence of the eigenvector definition plus M14 singularity; it is not the definition.

Define. Using the convention p_A(t)=det(A-tI), p_A is the characteristic polynomial. Its roots are the eigenvalues. Some books use det(tI-A); for an n×n matrix that differs by the factor (-1)^n and has the same roots.

Worked example. Let A=[[3,1],[1,3]]. Then A-tI=[[3-t,1],[1,3-t]], so p_A(t)=(3-t)^2-1=t^2-6t+8=(t-2)(t-4). Thus λ=2,4. For λ=4, A-4I=[[-1,1],[1,-1]], whose null space is span{(1,1)}. For λ=2, A-2I=[[1,1],[1,1]], whose null space is span{(1,-1)}. Direct multiplication verifies both eigenpairs.

Explain the logic chain. Nonzero eigenvector → nontrivial kernel of A-λI → shifted matrix singular → determinant zero. Solving the determinant only produces candidate λ values; the eigenspace calculation tells us the actual directions.

Guided practice. Let B=[[2,2],[1,3]]. Form p_B(t), factor it, find its real eigenvalues, and compute a basis for the eigenspace of the larger eigenvalue. Finish with a direct Bv=λv check.

Fade. Main requires the whole derivation/computation on a new matrix. Transfer supplies a plausible but invalid det(A)=λ shortcut and asks for diagnosis plus repair.

Distinction check. det(A) is one scalar attached to A. The eigenvalue condition uses det(A-λI)=0, an equation in the unknown λ. Never replace one with the other.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. p_B(t)=(2-t)(3-t)-2=t^2-5t+4=(t-1)(t-4), so λ=1,4. For λ=4, B-4I=[[-2,2],[1,-1]], giving x=y and E_4=span{(1,1)}. Indeed B(1,1)=(4,4).

sessions.title: Structure before expansion
sessions.focus: Read eigenvalues from diagonal/triangular structure through the characteristic determinant and use trace/determinant only as consistency checks, not as eigenspace information.
sessions.purpose: S03 established the general determinant route. S04 teaches when matrix structure simplifies that route and prevents useful scalar invariants from becoming counterfeit definitions or eigenvector recipes.
sessions.centralCapability: Exploit triangular structure to obtain eigenvalues without unnecessary expansion, then use trace/determinant checks within justified scope while still computing eigenspaces separately when directions are requested.
sessions.principalObstacle: Off-diagonal entries are assumed to change triangular eigenvalues, or matching trace/determinant values are treated as if they identify eigenvectors.
entryPrerequisites: M14 determinant of triangular matrices and trace/determinant computation
requiredOwnership: Derive that the eigenvalues of an exact triangular matrix are its diagonal entries by factoring det(A-λI).

Use trace and determinant as consistency checks on computed eigenvalues in the concrete small-matrix cases justified by the characteristic polynomial, without treating them as the definition of eigenvalues.
Reject the inference that correct eigenvalue checks determine eigenvectors; compute eigenspaces from A-λI when directional information is required.
sessions.applicationScope: Exact diagonal/triangular small matrices and 2×2 characteristic-polynomial checks.
sessions.transferScope: Audit a report whose eigenvalues pass trace/determinant checks but whose claimed coordinate-axis eigenvectors are false.
sessions.exitCondition: Recognize triangular eigenvalues structurally, check them economically, and refuse to infer eigendirections from scalar checks.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. S03 gives a universal small-matrix workflow, but expanding every determinant can hide structure. For triangular matrices the shifted matrix A-tI is still triangular, and M14 tells us its determinant is the product of its diagonal entries.

Derive. If U is upper triangular with diagonal d1,...,dn, then det(U-tI)=(d1-t)...(dn-t). Therefore the roots are exactly the diagonal values. The off-diagonal entries can change eigenspaces dramatically, but they do not change these triangular eigenvalues.

Worked example. Let U=[[2,7,0],[0,-1,4],[0,0,5]]. Then p_U(t)=(2-t)(-1-t)(5-t), so the eigenvalues are 2,-1,5. We did not ignore the off-diagonal entries by guesswork; the triangular determinant theorem made them irrelevant to this determinant.

Checks, not definitions. For a 2×2 matrix [[a,b],[c,d]], det(A-tI)=t^2-(a+d)t+(ad-bc). Thus after finding roots λ1,λ2, their sum should equal tr(A)=a+d and their product should equal det(A)=ad-bc. These are useful error checks in this scope. They do not tell us the eigenspace bases.

Worked check. For M=[[4,1],[2,3]], p_M(t)=t^2-7t+10=(t-5)(t-2). The roots sum to 7=tr(M) and multiply to 10=det(M). To get directions we would still solve Null(M-5I) and Null(M-2I).

Guided practice. Let B=[[3,10,-2],[0,4,9],[0,0,-2]]. Write p_B(t) directly from triangular structure, list its eigenvalues, and use the diagonal entries to check the trace and determinant numerically.

Fade. Main uses a new triangular 3×3 matrix. Transfer gives correct eigenvalues/checks but false eigenvectors, so scalar invariants cannot carry the answer.

Distinction check. A shortcut is legitimate when it follows from structure. A check can detect some arithmetic mistakes; it is not a substitute for the object you are trying to compute.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. p_B(t)=(3-t)(4-t)(-2-t), so the eigenvalues are 3,4,-2. Their sum is 5, matching tr(B)=5, and their product is -24, matching the triangular determinant 3·4·(-2)=-24.

sessions.title: Same eigenspace, different theorem
sessions.focus: Use eigenspace closure for equal eigenvalues and prove independence for eigenvectors carrying distinct eigenvalues.
sessions.purpose: Multiplicity and diagonalization will fail if the learner treats every collection of eigenvectors as automatically independent or treats linear combinations of different eigenmodes as one eigenmode.
sessions.centralCapability: Reason algebraically about linear combinations of eigenvectors, distinguishing closure inside one eigenspace from independence across distinct eigenvalues.
sessions.principalObstacle: Two true slogans are overgeneralized: 'eigenvectors form special directions' becomes 'all eigenvectors are independent', while 'linear combinations stay in a subspace' becomes 'any sum of eigenvectors is an eigenvector'.
entryPrerequisites: M13 linear independence and induction/proof habits from M03
requiredOwnership: Use linearity to show that a linear combination of vectors from the same E_λ remains in E_λ, with nonzero combinations giving eigenvectors for λ.
Reconstruct a proof that three nonzero eigenvectors associated with pairwise distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent.
Reject the claim that arbitrary eigenvectors must be independent, distinguishing the same-eigenvalue case from the distinct-eigenvalue theorem.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite real eigenvectors/eigenspaces; no multiplicity counts are yet named.
sessions.transferScope: Audit a dependence claim inside one eigenspace using a scalar-multiple counterexample and contrast it with the distinct-eigenvalue theorem.
sessions.exitCondition: Given eigenvectors and their eigenvalues, determine which linear-combination and independence conclusions are justified and prove the relevant one.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. S02 says E_λ is a subspace. That immediately gives one kind of linear-combination theorem. A different theorem applies when eigenvalues are distinct. Mixing the two is dangerous.

Same eigenvalue. If Au=λu and Aw=λw, then for any scalars a,b, A(au+bw)=aAu+bAw=λ(au+bw). Thus au+bw lies in E_λ. If that combination is nonzero, it is itself an eigenvector for λ; if it is zero, it is still in the eigenspace but is not an eigenvector.

Distinct eigenvalues: two-vector proof. Suppose Av=λv, Aw=μw with λ≠μ and av+bw=0. Apply A: aλv+bμw=0. Subtract μ(av+bw)=0 to get a(λ-μ)v=0. Since v≠0 and λ-μ≠0, a=0, then b=0. So v,w are independent.

Finite extension. The same idea proves that eigenvectors associated with pairwise distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent. For an induction step, start with c1v1+...+cnvn=0, apply A-λ_n I, and the vn term disappears. The remaining n-1 vectors still have distinct eigenvalues, so induction forces their coefficients to vanish, then cn=0.

Worked contrast. For A=2I, every nonzero vector is an eigenvector with λ=2. The pair e1 and 2e1 are both eigenvectors but dependent. The pair e1,e2 are both eigenvectors with the same λ and are independent. Same eigenvalue alone forces neither dependence nor independence; it says only that the vectors lie in one eigenspace.

Guided practice. Let B=[[2,1],[1,2]]. Verify v=(1,-1) has λ=1 and w=(1,1) has λ=3. Starting from av+bw=0, use the distinct-eigenvalue argument rather than a determinant to prove a=b=0. Then explain why v+w is not automatically an eigenvector.

Fade. Main moves to a symbolic three-vector proof plus a same-eigenvalue closure argument. Transfer gives a false universal-independence report and asks for the exact failed hypothesis.

Distinction check. 'Same eigenvalue' gives a subspace. 'Distinct eigenvalues' gives independence. Neither statement can be reversed without extra information.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. Bv=(1,-1)=v and Bw=(3,3)=3w. Apply B to av+bw=0 and subtract 3 times the original relation: a(1-3)v=0, so a=0, then b=0. Meanwhile v+w=(2,0), and B(2,0)=(4,2), not proportional to (2,0), so it is not an eigenvector.

sessions.title: Repeated roots are not repeated directions
sessions.focus: Separate algebraic multiplicity of a characteristic root from geometric multiplicity as eigenspace dimension, and use examples to diagnose repeated-eigenvalue overclaims.
sessions.purpose: S07 will decide whether enough eigenvectors exist to form a basis. Before that decision, the learner must stop treating polynomial repetition as a count of independent eigenvectors.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute algebraic and geometric multiplicities for exact small matrices and explain why the same characteristic polynomial can hide different eigenspace dimensions.
sessions.principalObstacle: A repeated factor (λ0-t)^k is read as 'k eigenvectors' without examining Null(A-λ0I).
requiredOwnership: Compute algebraic multiplicity from the multiplicity of an eigenvalue as a characteristic-polynomial root.
Compute geometric multiplicity as dim E_λ from an eigenspace basis.
Use concrete matrices to refute the inference that a repeated eigenvalue automatically supplies the same number of independent eigenvectors.
sessions.applicationScope: Exact 2×2/3×3 matrices with factorable characteristic polynomials.
sessions.transferScope: Audit a report that turns a double characteristic root into two independent directions without computing the eigenspace.
sessions.exitCondition: For each repeated eigenvalue of a small matrix, report both multiplicities and state what the polynomial does and does not imply about eigendirections.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. The characteristic polynomial can repeat a root. That repetition lives in a polynomial. Independent eigen-directions live in a vector space. We need two different numbers.

Define. The algebraic multiplicity a_λ is the multiplicity of λ as a root of the characteristic polynomial. The geometric multiplicity g_λ is dim(E_λ)=dim Null(A-λI). Because λ is an eigenvalue, g_λ≥1.

Support theorem. In finite dimensions, 1≤g_λ≤a_λ. We record this as a bounded standard support theorem here; S06 does not make its general proof an assessment obligation. The important immediate lesson is that equality need not hold.

Worked contrast. Let J=[[4,1],[0,4]]. Its characteristic polynomial is (4-t)^2, so a_4=2. But J-4I=[[0,1],[0,0]] has E_4=span{(1,0)}, so g_4=1. By contrast, K=4I_2 has the same characteristic polynomial (4-t)^2 but E_4=R^2, so g_4=2. Same polynomial; different eigenspace structure.

Connect. S03 tells us how many times a root appears. S02 tells us the dimension of the corresponding null space. Do both calculations before making a statement about independent eigenvectors.

Guided practice. Let B=diag(5,5,1). Compute p_B(t), a_5, E_5 and g_5. Then compare with J above: what does a_λ alone fail to tell you?

Fade. Main compares two fresh matrices with the same repeated root. Transfer gives a 3×3 report that explicitly converts a double root into 'two eigenvectors' and asks for the missing eigenspace calculation.

Distinction check. Algebraic multiplicity counts root repetition in p_A. Geometric multiplicity counts independent directions in E_λ. Never substitute one count for the other.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. p_B(t)=(5-t)^2(1-t), so a_5=2. Since B-5I=diag(0,0,-4), E_5=span{(1,0,0),(0,1,0)} and g_5=2. The same algebraic multiplicity 2 can therefore accompany g=1 or g=2.

sessions.title: When eigenvectors form a basis
sessions.focus: Characterize diagonalizability through an eigenbasis, use eigenspace dimensions to count available independent directions, and derive the distinct-eigenvalues corollary.
sessions.purpose: S08 will build diagonal coordinates only after S07 establishes when such coordinates exist. The learner must decide existence before manipulating P and D.
sessions.centralCapability: Determine whether a finite real matrix has enough independent eigenvectors to form a basis and justify diagonalizability without treating repeated eigenvalues as automatic success or failure.
sessions.principalObstacle: Repeated eigenvalues are used as a yes/no shortcut, or algebraic multiplicity is counted instead of actual eigenspace dimensions.
requiredOwnership: State and use the criterion that an n×n matrix is diagonalizable exactly when R^n has a basis of eigenvectors.
Use eigenspace bases/dimensions to decide whether enough independent eigenvectors exist, including a repeated-eigenvalue case that still diagonalizes.
Derive that n distinct real eigenvalues of an n×n real matrix guarantee diagonalizability by combining S05 independence with the basis-size criterion.
sessions.applicationScope: Exact finite real matrices whose real eigenspaces are computable from prior sessions.
sessions.transferScope: Audit a repeated-root non-diagonalizability claim when eigenspace data are supplied directly rather than through a matrix.
sessions.exitCondition: Given eigenvalue/eigenspace data, decide diagonalizability and defend the decision by basis/dimension rather than root-count folklore.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. We want coordinates in which A acts independently along coordinate axes. That is possible exactly when the space has a basis made of eigenvectors.

Define. An n×n real matrix A is diagonalizable over R when there is a basis of R^n consisting of real eigenvectors of A. Equivalently, A is similar to a diagonal matrix. S08 will construct the actual change-of-basis matrices; S07 owns the existence decision.

Count directions, not roots. Eigenspaces for distinct eigenvalues intersect only at 0 and their eigenvector bases combine independently. So the practical question is whether the dimensions of the distinct eigenspaces supply n independent directions. Repeated eigenvalues are allowed if their eigenspaces are large enough.

Worked example. D=diag(4,4,1) has λ=4 with E_4=span{e1,e2} and λ=1 with E_1=span{e3}. These three eigenvectors form a basis, so D is diagonalizable despite a repeated eigenvalue.

Distinct-eigenvalue corollary. If an n×n matrix has n distinct real eigenvalues, choose one nonzero eigenvector for each. S05 says those n vectors are independent; in R^n, n independent vectors form a basis. Therefore the matrix is diagonalizable.

Guided practice. Let B=[[2,1,0],[1,2,0],[0,0,3]]. Find the eigenvalues/eigenspace dimensions and decide whether B is diagonalizable. Pay attention to the repeated eigenvalue.

Fade. Main uses a different repeated-eigenvalue matrix and asks for the general distinct-root corollary. Transfer removes the matrix entirely and gives only characteristic/eigenspace data, so the learner must reason from the capability contract rather than repeat an elimination pattern.

Distinction check. Algebraic multiplicity counts roots. Diagonalizability asks for a basis of actual eigenvectors. A repeated root is compatible with either outcome.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. The 2×2 block has eigenvalues 3 and 1, while the third coordinate contributes another λ=3. E_3=span{(1,1,0),(0,0,1)} has dimension 2 and E_1=span{(1,-1,0)} has dimension 1. Together they supply three independent eigenvectors, so B is diagonalizable.

sessions.title: Build the diagonal coordinates
sessions.focus: Construct P and D from an ordered eigenbasis, derive AP=PD and A=PDP^-1, and enforce column/eigenvalue order consistency.
sessions.purpose: S07 decides whether an eigenbasis exists. S08 turns that basis into an explicit similarity transformation and makes the algebraic identity follow from column action rather than memorization.
sessions.centralCapability: Given an ordered eigenbasis and matching eigenvalues, build and verify a diagonalization with correct column/eigenvalue correspondence.
sessions.principalObstacle: P and D are assembled independently, so eigenvalue order is mismatched to eigenvector columns; or A=PDP^-1 is quoted without understanding AP=PD.
entryPrerequisites: M14 matrix multiplication, inverse and similarity
requiredOwnership: Construct P from ordered eigenvector columns and D from the corresponding eigenvalues in the same order.
Derive AP=PD columnwise and hence A=PDP^-1 using invertibility of the eigenbasis matrix P.
Detect and repair a diagonalization whose P-column order and D-diagonal order do not match.
sessions.applicationScope: Exact small real diagonalizable matrices with explicitly computable eigenbases.
sessions.transferScope: Audit a mismatched P,D pair on a different matrix by comparing AP and PD rather than trusting the symbols.
sessions.exitCondition: Construct a correct diagonalization and diagnose an order mismatch from the defining column relations.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. S07 says an eigenbasis exists. Put those basis vectors into a matrix so the basis change becomes explicit.

Define. Let v1,...,vn be an ordered eigenbasis with Avi=λivi. Form P=[v1 ... vn] and D=diag(λ1,...,λn) in the same order. Because the columns of P are a basis, P is invertible.

Derive columnwise. The j-th column of AP is Avj=λjvj. The j-th column of PD is also λjvj because D scales column j of P by λj. Hence AP=PD. Right-multiplying by P^-1 gives A=PDP^-1.

Worked example. For A=[[4,1],[0,2]], v4=(1,0) and v2=(-1,2). Thus P=[[1,-1],[0,2]], D=diag(4,2). Direct multiplication gives AP=PD; since P^-1=[[1,1/2],[0,1/2]], PDP^-1=A.

Order warning. If the columns of P are swapped, the diagonal entries of D must be swapped too. The equation AP=PD is the quickest audit because it checks each column-eigenvalue pairing.

Guided practice. Let B=[[3,1],[0,2]]. Use v3=(1,0) and v2=(-1,1) to build P,D, derive AP=PD for B, compute P^-1 and verify B=PDP^-1.

Fade. Main uses a new matrix and requires the full construction. Transfer provides a plausible mismatched pair and asks the learner to locate exactly which columns/eigenvalues are paired incorrectly.

Distinction check. Diagonalization is a basis-change statement. D does not belong to A independently of the ordered eigenbasis used to build P.

sessions.title: Powers without brute force
sessions.focus: Derive A^k=PD^kP^-1 for a diagonalizable matrix and use diagonal powers for exact finite repeated action.
sessions.purpose: S01 handled repeated action only along one eigenvector. S09 upgrades that idea to the whole space once S08 has built eigen-coordinates.
sessions.centralCapability: Use a valid diagonalization to derive and compute integer matrix powers, and apply the result to a finite discrete update without repeated matrix multiplication.
sessions.principalObstacle: The learner memorizes A^k=PD^kP^-1 without seeing the cancellation, raises P or P^-1 to powers unnecessarily, or applies the formula when diagonalization has not been established.
requiredOwnership: Use the P^-1P cancellation mechanism to justify A^m=PD^mP^-1 for a specified nonnegative integer exponent m from a valid diagonalization.
Compute an exact finite matrix power from a supplied/constructed diagonalization.
Translate a finite recurrence x_{k+1}=Ax_k into eigen-coordinates and compute a requested state without step-by-step iteration.
sessions.applicationScope: Exact finite powers of small real diagonalizable matrices; k is a nonnegative integer.
sessions.transferScope: Change from a matrix-power request to a state-update recurrence whose initial condition must be decomposed into eigenmodes.
sessions.exitCondition: Given a justified diagonalization, compute A^k or a finite x_k structurally and state why the formula is legal.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. S08 gives A=PDP^-1. Multiplying A by itself seems to create many factors, but the change-of-basis matrices cancel in pairs.

Derive. A^2=(PDP^-1)(PDP^-1)=PD(P^-1P)DP^-1=PD^2P^-1. Repeating gives A^k=PD^kP^-1 for every integer k≥0, with A^0=I=PIP^-1. Only the diagonal entries of D need to be powered.

Worked example. Let A=[[2,1],[1,2]]. Eigenvectors v3=(1,1), v1=(1,-1) give P=[[1,1],[1,-1]], D=diag(3,1), P^-1=(1/2)[[1,1],[1,-1]]. Therefore A^k=(1/2)[[3^k+1,3^k-1],[3^k-1,3^k+1]]. The formula comes from a valid diagonalization, not from pattern matching powers.

Connect to states. If x0=Pc gives eigen-coordinate vector c, then x_k=A^kx0=PD^kP^-1Pc=PD^kc. Each coordinate is scaled by its own λ_i^k.

Guided practice. Let C=[[4,0],[1,3]], with eigenvectors v4=(1,1), v3=(0,1). Decompose x0=(2,3) into these two eigenvectors and compute x3 from modal powers rather than three updates.

Fade. Main asks for a full fourth matrix power on new data. Transfer removes the explicit A^k request and gives a recurrence/initial state, so the learner must recognize the same structure.

Distinction check. The power formula is conditional: it follows from a valid diagonalization. It is not available merely because a matrix has some eigenvalues.

sessions.title: When the eigenvectors are not enough
sessions.focus: Diagnose defective matrices from insufficient eigenspace dimension and explain why no invertible eigenvector matrix can be manufactured by duplicating directions.
sessions.purpose: S07/S08 describe successful diagonalization. S10 makes failure a positive structural diagnosis rather than a computational accident and closes the door to fake P matrices.
sessions.centralCapability: Determine that a matrix is defective because its eigenspaces do not supply a full basis, and explain why ordinary diagonalization cannot be repaired by repeating dependent eigenvectors.
sessions.principalObstacle: Known eigenvalues are mistaken for a guarantee of enough eigenvectors; when a direction is missing, the learner duplicates a vector or chooses a scalar multiple to fill P.
entryPrerequisites: S08 P invertible iff its eigenvector columns form a basis
requiredOwnership: Diagnose a finite real matrix as defective when its eigenspaces supply fewer than n independent eigenvectors.
Explain why defectiveness prevents an invertible eigenvector matrix P and therefore ordinary A=PDP^-1 diagonalization.
Reject attempts to fill a missing eigendirection by duplicating an eigenvector or inserting a scalar multiple of an existing one.
sessions.applicationScope: Exact small real matrices with computed/supplied eigenspaces; no generalized eigenvectors.
sessions.transferScope: Audit an abstract data-only proposal that duplicates an eigendirection to manufacture a square P.
sessions.exitCondition: Recognize and prove ordinary diagonalization failure from eigenspace dimension, without inventing missing modes.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. A matrix can have all of its eigenvalues known and still fail to have enough eigenvectors for an eigenbasis. That failure is structural, not a bad choice of arithmetic.

Define. An n×n matrix is defective when it is not diagonalizable because it lacks n linearly independent eigenvectors. Equivalently, the combined eigenspaces do not supply a basis of the whole space.

Worked example. J=[[2,1],[0,2]] has p_J(t)=(2-t)^2, but E_2=span{(1,0)} has dimension 1. R^2 needs two independent basis vectors, so J is defective. Trying P=[e1,2e1] gives two columns but only one direction; P is singular and cannot be inverted.

Contrast. 2I_2 has the same characteristic polynomial but E_2=R^2, so it is not defective. Eigenvalues alone do not determine diagonalizability.

Why duplication cannot help. P must implement a basis change. Repeating a vector or inserting a scalar multiple leaves the columns dependent, so the map from eigen-coordinates back to the original coordinates is not invertible. The missing direction is mathematical information we do not possess.

Guided practice. Let C=[[5,2,0],[0,5,0],[0,0,-1]]. Compute E_5 and E_-1, total their dimensions, decide whether C is defective, and explain what goes wrong with any 3-column P built only from those eigenspaces.

Fade. Main uses a lower-triangular defective matrix. Transfer removes matrix arithmetic entirely and presents only eigenspace data plus a fake duplicated-column P.

Distinction check. 'Three eigenvalues counted with multiplicity' is not 'three independent eigenvectors.' A square array of eigenvector columns is not automatically a basis matrix.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. E_5=span{(1,0,0)} has dimension 1 and E_-1=span{(0,0,1)} has dimension 1, so only two independent eigendirections are available in R^3. C is defective. Any third column chosen from those same one-dimensional spaces is dependent on an existing column, so P is singular.

sessions.title: Same operator, different coordinates
sessions.focus: Prove that similarity preserves the characteristic polynomial/eigenvalues while eigenvector coordinate lists transform with the basis change.
sessions.purpose: M14 introduced similar matrices as different coordinate representations of one linear operator. M16 now identifies which spectral data survive that representation change and which coordinate objects change.
sessions.centralCapability: Given B=S^-1AS, prove spectral invariance and correctly transform eigenvector coordinates instead of claiming similar matrices have identical eigenvector lists.
sessions.principalObstacle: Similarity is misread as elementwise sameness: if eigenvalues are preserved, learners often assume the same coordinate vector is an eigenvector of both matrices.
entryPrerequisites: M14 similar matrices/change of basis and determinant multiplicativity
requiredOwnership: Prove det(B-tI)=det(A-tI) when B=S^-1AS, hence similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial and eigenvalues.
Transform an eigenvector coordinate vector v of A into S^-1v for B and verify the corresponding eigenvalue is unchanged.
Reject the claim that similar matrices must have identical eigenvector coordinate lists.
sessions.applicationScope: Exact finite real similar matrices with an explicitly supplied invertible change-of-basis matrix.
sessions.transferScope: Audit a same-eigenvector-coordinate claim on a different similar pair and repair it by transforming coordinates.
sessions.exitCondition: Distinguish operator-level spectral invariants from basis-dependent eigenvector coordinates and prove the transformation law.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. M14 taught that B=S^-1AS can represent the same linear operator in different coordinates. What does eigentheory keep, and what changes?

Characteristic polynomial. Since I=S^-1S, B-tI=S^-1AS-tS^-1S=S^-1(A-tI)S. Taking determinants and using M14 multiplicativity gives det(B-tI)=det(S^-1)det(A-tI)det(S)=det(A-tI). Thus similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial and the same eigenvalues with the same root multiplicities.

Eigenvector coordinates. If Av=λv, define w=S^-1v. Then Bw=S^-1AS(S^-1v)=S^-1Av=λS^-1v=λw. So the same operator-level eigendirection is represented by transformed coordinates; the coordinate list generally changes.

Worked example. Let A=diag(2,3) and S=[[1,1],[0,1]]. Then S^-1=[[1,-1],[0,1]] and B=S^-1AS=[[2,-1],[0,3]]. The A-eigenvector e2 for λ=3 becomes S^-1e2=(-1,1), and indeed B(-1,1)=3(-1,1). The eigenvalue stayed 3; the coordinate vector changed.

Guided practice. Let A=diag(1,4), S=[[1,0],[1,1]], and B=S^-1AS. Compute B, transform e1 and e2 using S^-1, and verify both B-eigenpairs. Then confirm the characteristic polynomials agree without expanding both from scratch.

Fade. Main requires both invariance proofs and transformed eigenvectors on fresh data. Transfer starts from a false “same eigenvectors” report and asks for one direct countercheck plus the correct transformed coordinates.

Distinction check. Similarity preserves operator-level spectral data such as characteristic polynomial/eigenvalues. A coordinate column vector is representation-dependent.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. S^-1=[[1,0],[-1,1]], B=[[1,0],[3,4]]. e1 (λ=1) becomes (1,-1), and e2 (λ=4) stays (0,1). Direct multiplication verifies both. The determinant identity gives the same characteristic polynomial automatically.

sessions.title: A real matrix can have nonreal modes
sessions.focus: Introduce only the complex-number language needed to interpret nonreal eigenvalues of real matrices, conjugate pairs, and the distinction between real and complex eigendirections.
sessions.purpose: S13 will prove that real symmetric matrices avoid nonreal eigenvalues. Before that contrast is meaningful, the learner needs a bounded bridge showing that an arbitrary real matrix may have no real eigenvector even though it has complex eigenpairs.
sessions.centralCapability: Solve a simple characteristic equation with negative discriminant using i, verify a complex eigenpair for a real matrix, and state the scalar field when saying whether eigenvalues/eigenvectors exist.
sessions.principalObstacle: 'No real roots' is inflated into 'no eigenvalues', or complex eigenvalues are treated as evidence that the original matrix entries must be complex.
entryPrerequisites: M02 quadratic algebra over the reals
S01 distinction between real eigendirection and fixed vector
requiredOwnership: Use i^2=-1 to solve a simple quadratic characteristic equation with negative real discriminant and identify the conjugate eigenvalue pair.
Verify a supplied/constructed complex eigenvector for a real matrix by direct matrix-vector multiplication.
Distinguish 'no real eigenvalue/eigenvector' from 'no eigenvalue over C' and state the scalar field explicitly.
sessions.applicationScope: 2×2 real matrices with simple conjugate imaginary eigenvalues; only minimal complex arithmetic.
sessions.transferScope: Audit a report that mistakes absence of real characteristic roots for absence of eigenvalues over the complex numbers.
inScope: complex conjugate roots for real polynomials
sessions.exitCondition: Handle a simple nonreal eigenpair honestly and qualify eigenvalue statements by R versus C.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. S01 showed that a real linear map can fail to preserve any nonzero real direction. The characteristic equation now tells us what may still exist if we enlarge the scalar field.

Minimal bridge. Define i by i^2=-1. A complex number is a+bi with real a,b. For a polynomial with real coefficients, nonreal roots occur in conjugate pairs: if p(z)=0, then p(conj(z))=conj(p(z))=0. We use only this amount of complex arithmetic here.

Worked example. Let A=[[0,-4],[1,0]]. Then p_A(t)=det(A-tI)=t^2+4, so over R there are no eigenvalues. Over C, t=±2i. For λ=2i, v=(2i,1) is nonzero and A v=(-4,2i)=2i(2i,1), so it is a complex eigenvector. The conjugate vector (-2i,1) works for -2i.

Interpret carefully. The matrix A is still real. The complex pair describes structure that cannot be represented by a real invariant line. For real two-dimensional dynamics such pairs are associated with rotational/oscillatory behaviour, but M16 does not build a full complex dynamical theory here.

Guided practice. Let B=[[0,-1],[4,0]]. Compute p_B(t), solve its roots over C, and verify one complex eigenvector. State separately what is true over R and over C.

Fade. Main uses a different scale and asks for both roots and one verified complex eigenvector. Transfer begins with a false domain conclusion and requires field-qualified repair.

Distinction check. 'A is a real matrix' describes its entries. 'A has only real eigenvalues' is an additional property and is false for arbitrary real matrices.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. p_B(t)=t^2+4, so the roots are ±2i. For λ=2i, v=(1,-2i) works because Bv=(2i,4)=2i(1,-2i). Over R there is no eigenvalue/eigenvector; over C there are two eigenvalues with complex eigenvectors.
